content: Lavandula angustifolia, also known as Lavandula spica or Lavandula vera, is commonly referred to as Common Lavender or True Lavender. Despite being inaccurately called English Lavender in some regions, it is not native to England. This plant belongs to the Lamiaceae family and is indigenous to the western Mediterranean region, particularly the Pyrenees and other mountainous areas in northern Spain. It is a highly aromatic shrub that typically grows to a height of 1 to 2 meters. The leaves are evergreen, measuring 2 to 6 cm in length and 4 to 6 mm in width. The flowers are pinkish-purple, often described as lavender-colored, and are borne on spikes that are 2 to 8 cm long. These spikes are located at the top of slender, leafless stems that range from 10 to 30 cm in length. Lavandula angustifolia is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant due to its vibrant flowers, pleasant fragrance, and ability to thrive with minimal water requirements. However, it does not tolerate persistently damp soil conditions. It is relatively cold-hardy and is generally considered suitable for growth in USDA hardiness zone 5. Beyond its ornamental value, the flowers and leaves of Lavandula angustifolia are utilized in herbal medicine. They are commonly processed into lavender oil or brewed as herbal tea. The flowers are also employed as a culinary herb, most notably as a component of the French herb blend known as herbes de Provence. Lavender essential oil, when diluted with a carrier oil, is frequently used in massage therapy as a relaxant. Additionally, lavender-based products such as lotions, eye pillows filled with lavender flowers or essential oil, and bath oils are often used to promote relaxation and alleviate stress.
